extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom managers, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for distinguishing and classifying news stories along a hard–soft continuum, listing topic categories, stylistic/focus dimensions, and newsworthiness criteria to guide editorial decisions and story treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard News Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: "Breaking news and up-to-the-minute news about serious, timely, or hard-hitting topics that are timely and urgent, usually based on facts and rigorous research."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames hard news as fact-based, urgent, serious, and research-driven; implies emphasis on public importance and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: "Journalistic style and genre that blurs the line between information and entertainment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes soft news as entertainment-leaning, human-centered, and less urgent; signals different audience expectations and editorial placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-Dimension Hardness Scale — Topic dimension
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with politically relevant subject matter score as 'harder' on the hardness scale; topic selection is a primary axis of hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-Dimension Hardness Scale — Focus dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus dimension — focuses on societal consequences
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A focus on societal-level consequences (policy, public impact) increases hardness; individual-focused stories lower hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-Dimension Hardness Scale — Style dimension
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impersonal, unemotional reporting style (vs. personal/emotional tone) contributes to a 'hard' treatment; narrative, emotional styles move toward 'soft.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard News Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Government and politics; Economics and business; International relations; Welfare and policy; Scientific developments; Crime; Public safety; Disasters; Major court decisions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are topic areas typically treated as hard news because of their public importance, policy relevance, or societal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrity; Lifestyle; Entertainment; Human interest; Consumer products; Travel; Food; Fashion; Sports (some treatments); Health (lifestyle-side)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics that tend to invite personal, emotional, or entertainment-oriented framing; some topics (e.g., sports, health) can be treated either way depending on focus and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of urgency and immediacy; breaking developments and rapidly evolving events increase hard-news value and editorial priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact on policy or large groups
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that affect policies or large populations rate higher in hardness and news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public significance (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance to public affairs, civic life, or functioning of institutions; a core determinant of hard-news priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude of consequence (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale and seriousness of outcomes (e.g., loss of life, economic harm) increase newsworthiness and justify hard framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power involved (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involvement of government, corporations, or other powerful actors elevates a story's hardness and public-interest justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with civic stakes (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts that implicate civic values, governance, or public interest increase hard-news priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to check facts and substantiate claims is central to hard news; demands rigorous sourcing and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility (Hard-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability and authority of sources affect whether a story is treated as hard news and how prominently it is placed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal stories that evoke empathy or curiosity; a primary driver of soft-news selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional resonance (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that trigger emotions (joy, sadness, admiration) are characteristic of soft news and attract audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifiable subject (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of a clear, relatable person or character around whom the story is built increases soft-news appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / oddity (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel, odd, or quirky elements make stories more entertaining and shareable—key soft-news criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspirational value (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that uplift or inspire audiences are often pursued as soft features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual appeal (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong visual elements (images, scenes) increase soft-news suitability, especially for broadcast and digital platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifestyle relevance (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, consumer-oriented, or lifestyle-focused relevance drives soft-news utility journalism and service pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural moment (Soft-news newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tapping into zeitgeist or trending cultural topics boosts soft-news prominence and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard and soft news exist on a continuum rather than as distinct categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same topic can be treated as harder or softer depending on focus and style (e.g., climate through policy analysis vs. personal narrative); soft stories can carry political information and hard topics can be softened. Use the continuum to judge treatment rather than rigid labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement and presentation differ: hard news typically goes A1/lead segment while soft news runs inside, later segments, or weekends; tabloids may lead with soft framing of hard topics; quality press leads with hard; digital platforms mix by audience segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hardness assessment to inform placement, headline framing, segment position, and platform targeting; audience and mission shape the hard/soft balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of hybrid genres such as political infotainment, celebrity politics, disaster human interest, service journalism, explainer + feature, personal essay + analysis
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and intentionally design hybrids — they combine hard informational elements with soft storytelling techniques and require careful editorial choices about balance, sourcing, and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit newsworthiness tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news prioritizes importance while soft news prioritizes interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best journalism finds intersections of importance and interest; editorial choices reflect mission (push toward hard) and audience demand (trend toward soft).
